The project began with a full structural and mechanical assessment, followed by corrosion treatment, boiler and steam-system refurbishment, refitting of worn running gear, and sympathetic repainting to preserve the machine’s original character. Where original components could not be safely reused, period-appropriate replacements were fabricated to maintain historical integrity. The restored shovel now demonstrates the operation and appearance of the machine as it would have worked at the Black Mountain strip in 1950.

Restoration notes:
- Initial assessment: documented chassis, boom, bucket, boiler, and controls
- Disassembly: removed and labeled major assemblies for inspection
- Metalwork: repaired corrosion and reinforced structural members
- Steam system: inspected and overhauled boiler, piping, and valves
- Mechanical: refurbished gearing, bearings, and track assemblies
- Reassembly and testing: aligned systems, performed static and low-pressure tests
- Finishing: applied historically appropriate paint and placards

Attachments: restoration photos and spec sheet attached.

Regards,

style_agnostic:
Listen here, Grandson,

I want to tell you about ham radio as a useful hobby and an emergency tool. When I was on the road, having a radio kept me in touch and helped me when I needed it.

Do this:
1. Getting licensed: study for the entry-level amateur radio license, find a local class or online course, register for an exam session, and pass the test to get your call sign.
2. Buying starter gear: start with a simple handheld transceiver (HT), a basic antenna, a spare battery and charger, and a case; buy from a known seller and keep your receipts.
3. Practicing nets: listen to local nets first, then check in regularly, follow net control instructions, practice clear brief transmissions, and learn net etiquette.
4. Using radio in emergencies: keep your radio charged and accessible, have basic power and antenna options ready, know local repeaters and emergency channels, practice short status messages, and coordinate with others when phone service fails.

Love,
Grandpa

Listen here, grandson/granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I learned a few simple things to keep you safe and moving during winter work and cold-weather hauling. Follow these practical steps.

Do this:
- Antifreeze: check concentration and top off to the proper level; use the correct type for your engine and test with a coolant tester.
- Battery checks: clean terminals, tighten connections, check voltage/load, and replace any weak batteries before a cold snap.
- Fuel additives: use the recommended anti-gel or winter fuel additive for your fuel type and keep the tank at least half full to reduce condensation.
- Heater maintenance: test the cabin heater and defroster, inspect hoses and belts, replace clogged cabin filters, and fix any leaks before you go.
- Cold-weather clothing/safety: dress in layers, wear insulated waterproof boots, warm gloves and a hat; carry an emergency kit with blankets, food, water, flashlight and a phone charger.

Love, Grandpa

task_details: Audience: grandson/granddaughter. Include an opening 'Listen here,' and the phrase 'When I was on the road,'. Provide step-by-step 'Do this:' checklist covering walk-around, lights, tires, brakes, fluids, trailer coupling, and paperwork. Use plain elder-on-the-job tone. End with 'Love' or name.
personalized: Listen here, you gotta learn to spot trouble before it finds you. When I was on the road, a quick walk-around saved me more than once. Do this: walk the perimeter and look for leaks or loose straps; check tire pressure and sidewalls; test all lights and turn signals; pinch the brake lines and check brake drums for hot spots; check fluid levels—oil, coolant, power steering; make sure the fifth wheel is locked and safety chains are secure; confirm load is tied down and paperwork is in the cab. Do these same checks every morning. Don’t skip it 'cause you’re in a hurry. Love, Roy
style_agnostic:
Listen here, Grandson/Granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I did these checks every time. Plain and simple — do this:

Do this:
- Walk-around: inspect the whole rig and trailer for damage, loose cargo, open doors, hanging wires or anything out of place.
- Lights: test headlights, taillights, brake lights, turn signals, marker/clearance lights and hazards; fix or report any that don’t work.
- Tires: check pressure, look for cuts, bulges or uneven tread, ensure lug nuts look tight and no missing valve caps.
- Brakes: listen and feel for leaks or dragging, check air/hydraulic gauges and parking brake; do a slow brake test before you merge.
- Fluids: check oil, coolant, power steering and washer fluid levels; look under the truck for fresh leaks.
- Trailer coupling: confirm kingpin/locking jaws are seated and locked, latch/hood secure, safety chains and breakaway cable attached, electrical plug locked, landing gear stowed.
- Paperwork: have your license, registration, permits, logbook/ELD, bill of lading and pre-trip inspection report; note any defects before you leave.

Drive careful out there.

Love, Grandpa

Listen here, my granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I learned the value of simple habits that keep you steady. You're starting work now, so listen to an old head:

Do this:
- Budgeting: Write down your take-home pay and list fixed essentials (rent, food, transport). Set limits for discretionary spending and review the numbers each month. Pay yourself first by assigning a fixed amount or percentage to savings as soon as you’re paid.
- Emergency fund: Start by saving $1,000 as quickly as you can, then build toward roughly three months of essential expenses. Keep this money in a separate, easy-access account so it’s there for real emergencies.
- Avoiding bad debt: Don’t carry balances on high-interest cards; if you use credit, pay it off each month. Say no to payday loans and any offers that charge heavy interest. Only borrow when necessary and when you can afford the payments.
- Small regular saving habits: Automate transfers to savings on payday, set aside a small fixed amount each week, and increase that amount when your pay goes up. Treat saving like a non-negotiable bill.

Love, Grandma

style_agnostic:
Dear Grandson/Granddaughter,

Listen here, I want to teach you a few plain steps for doing family history using what’s nearby and what people remember. Keep it simple and steady — start with people and local records, not the web alone.

When I was on the road, I learned that a name and a story often live in somebody’s kitchen. Talk to our older relatives; they hold dates, places, nicknames and little facts that the papers don’t write down.

Do this:
1. Interviewing relatives:
   - Make a list of questions before you go: names, dates, places, occupations, stories, nicknames.
   - Visit in person when you can. Sit, listen, and let them tell stories. Record the conversation or take careful notes.
   - Ask where they got their information and whether they remember documents, letters, photos, or Bibles.
   - Note who said what, and the date you spoke with them.

2. Checking county courthouse records:
   - Go to the county courthouse for deeds, wills, probate, marriage records, and land records.
   - Ask the clerk where records are kept and how to order copies or look at indexes.
   - Make copies or take clear photos of original records and write down the book and page, file number, or case number.

3. Cemeteries:
   - Visit local cemeteries and churchyards. Look for family plots and read headstones for names and dates.
   - Take photos of inscriptions and note the cemetery name, section, and plot location.
   - If a stone is unreadable, jot down what you can and ask cemetery staff or local historical groups for help.

4. Documenting sources:
   - For every fact you collect, write down where you found it: who told you, which courthouse book, which cemetery, or which file.
   - Date your notes and keep copies of documents and photos in a named folder.
   - Even simple notes about where a story came from will help later when you try to prove details.

Do these steps patiently, one relative and one record at a time. Keep your notes clear and save copies of what you find. That way the next generation won’t have to start over.

Love,
Grandma

I’ll show you how to spot a real miner’s lamp. Love, Roy
style_agnostic:
Listen here, Dear Grandson/Granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I learned a few simple truths about picking up antiques and mining memorabilia at flea markets. It’s mostly about paying attention, being polite, and using your common sense. Here’s how to do it.

Do this:
- Research first: spend a little time online or at the library before you go. Know rough prices, maker names, common marks, and the local mining history so you can tell a true piece from a pretty fake. Take notes or photos on your phone so you know what to look for.
- Inspect carefully: handle things gently, look for repairs, cracks, missing parts, replaced screws, and fresh paint that hides damage. Check bottoms and backs for stamps or maker’s marks. Smell for mustiness or chemicals. If it feels too light or too perfect, be suspicious.
- Bargain politely: smile, be friendly, and start lower than your top price. Point out real flaws instead of making wild accusations. Offer cash if you can, bundle items for a better deal, and know when to walk away — sometimes the best price comes after you’ve turned and left.
- Check provenance: ask the seller where they got it, get any paperwork or photos they have, and note serial numbers or maker marks. If the story doesn’t add up or the seller is vague, be careful. Provenance matters for value and for knowing you’re not buying something stolen.
- Think about transport: measure big items before you buy, bring blankets or padding, rope or straps, and have someone to help lift heavy things. Consider whether it will fit in your car or if you’ll need to arrange pickup or shipping, and factor that cost into your offer.

Trust your eyes and your gut, and treat people with respect — you’ll learn more and end up with better finds that way.

Love, Grandpa

style_agnostic:
Listen here, Grandson/Granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I learned how to price small landscaping and hauling jobs so you don’t sell yourself short. Below is straightforward business guidance you can use as a side business.

Do this:
1. Estimating labor: calculate the total hours for the job including setup and cleanup, add travel time, and multiply by a realistic hourly rate that compensates your time and skill.
2. Equipment: list required tools and vehicle use, include rental fees or amortized purchase cost, plus maintenance and wear; divide these costs across jobs to get a per-job equipment charge.
3. Fuel: estimate round-trip mileage and on-site driving, divide miles by your vehicle MPG and multiply by current fuel price; include fuel for power equipment if applicable.
4. Profit margin: choose a target margin (for example 15–30%) and apply it to your total direct costs to set a final price that leaves room for profit.
5. Paperwork: obtain any required local permits or licenses, provide written estimates and invoices, keep receipts and job records, and confirm any necessary insurance or liability coverage.
6. Customer terms: state payment terms (deposit amount and due dates), cancellation and rescheduling policy, how change orders are handled, and the scope/warranty in writing.

Keep estimates conservative, communicate terms clearly before you start, and adjust pricing as you gain experience.

Love

Listen here, my dear grandchild,

I want to offer some advice on balancing community involvement, our church, and running your small business. There is warmth and purpose in all three, but they can tug you in different directions. When I was on the road, I learned how important it is to protect time and to lean on others.

Do this:
- set boundaries — decide your work hours and protect them so community and church time don't eat into your business's needs.
- schedule community time — put community events on your calendar so they are planned, not accidental.
- use church for network and help — let the church be a place to find volunteers, mentors, and practical support.
- maintain work-life balance — rest, family, and faith need attention too; don't let work be the only thing.

I'll always be proud of how you care for others while building something of your own.

Love, Grandma

style_agnostic:
Listen here, grandson/granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I picked up a few simple rules about propane and gas grills. Follow them every time you grill or do small jobs.

Do this:
- Leak checks: before each use inspect hoses and connections for cracks or wear. Open the tank valve slightly and apply soapy water to fittings; bubbles mean a leak — shut it off, tighten or replace parts and don’t use until fixed.
- Ignition safety: keep the lid open when lighting; make sure burner controls are off before you open the tank; use the grill’s ignition or a long lighter and stand back. If it fails to light, turn the gas off, wait a few minutes, then try again.
- Grill placement: set the grill on a flat, stable, noncombustible surface well away from the house, railings, eaves, and anything that can catch fire. Never use a grill indoors or in enclosed spaces.
- Cleaning: scrape and brush grates after use, empty grease trays and remove buildup regularly to reduce flare-ups.
- Storage of cylinders: close the cylinder valve, keep cylinders upright in a ventilated outdoor area away from heat and direct sun; don’t store spare cylinders under the grill or inside.

Keep it simple and do these checks every time.

Love,
Grandpa

Dear Grandson/Granddaughter,

Listen here, I want you to learn how to document and preserve our local coal mining artifacts and the stories that go with them. When I was on the road, I realized how quickly things can be lost if they aren’t cared for.

Do this:
1) Cleaning and labeling artifacts:
   - Gently remove loose dirt with a soft brush or dry cloth; avoid soaking or harsh chemicals.
   - If an item is fragile, do not force anything — leave it to a conservator.
   - Attach an archival tag or paper tag to each piece; write in pencil or archival pen the item name, who it belonged to, where found, and date.

2) Photographing:
   - Photograph each item on a plain background from multiple angles.
   - Include a ruler or common object for scale and take close-ups of marks or labels.
   - Save image files with filenames that match the artifact label (e.g., 1920_pick_head_JohnSmith.jpg).

3) Recording interviews:
   - Use a phone or audio recorder in a quiet room; start by stating the speaker’s name, date, and location.
   - Ask open questions about memories, names, dates, and places; let them tell the story.
   - Back up audio files and note who is in each recording and any permissions to share.

4) Storing in dry conditions:
   - Store cleaned and labeled items in boxes or bins in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight.
   - Use silica gel packets or other desiccants to reduce moisture and check periodically for dampness.
   - Keep paper and photographs in acid-free folders or sleeves.

5) Sharing copies with the local museum:
   - Make copies of photos and audio files (and duplicates of documents) and label them clearly.
   - Deliver or email the copies to the local museum and keep a set for the family.
   - Keep a simple inventory list of what you shared and when.

Love,
Grandpa

Subject: Load securement plan for salvaged mine equipment — Pickup Friday 8:00 AM

Confirming load securement plan for pickup on Friday at 8:00 AM.

Salvaged items and weights:
- 3 cast-iron winch housings — est. 1,200 lb each
- 2 wooden crates — 400 lb each

Trailer: 20-foot trailer with side rails

Load placement:
- Place all items on the trailer centerline (longitudinal orientation) to keep load centered between side rails.
- Winch housings: place three units evenly spaced longitudinally at approximately 6 ft, 10 ft, and 14 ft from the front of the trailer.
- Wooden crates: place one crate forward at approximately 2 ft from the front and one crate aft at approximately 18 ft from the front.

Center of gravity:
- Estimated overall center of gravity for the loaded trailer: approximately 9.5–10 ft from the front of the trailer (near midspan, slightly forward of midpoint), located on the trailer centerline.

Number of straps (minimum 6 required):
- Total straps to be used: 8 ratchet straps.
  - Winch housings: 2 straps per housing × 3 housings = 6 straps
  - Wooden crates: 1 strap per crate × 2 crates = 2 straps

Chain sizes:
- Winch housings: 3 × 3/8" Grade 70 transport chains (one chain available per housing for supplemental restraint)
- Wooden crates: 2 × 5/16" Grade 70 chains (one per crate)

Blocking:
- Provide wooden blocking under each item: two 4"x4" blocks fore and aft under each winch housing and each crate to bear on trailer floor and prevent vertical and lateral shift.
- Use wedge/keystone blocking at each end of every item against the blocks to prevent longitudinal movement.

Strap inventory (to be provided with the truck):
- 6 × 2" ratchet straps (30 ft) — allocated to winch housings (2 per housing)
- 2 × 2" ratchet straps (15–20 ft) — allocated to wooden crates (1 per crate)
- 3 × 3/8" Grade 70 transport chains — for winch housings
- 2 × 5/16" Grade 70 chains — for wooden crates
- Assorted 4"x4" blocking and wedges

Please confirm and advise if any changes are required.

Listen here, Grandson/Granddaughter,

When I was on the road, I learned how to move heavy items by myself. Do this:
- Plan lift: check the weight, clear the path, and decide where the item will go before you start.
- Use leverage: use a pry bar or long board to lift an edge and slide a dolly or rollers underneath.
- Straps: use strong straps to hold the load to the dolly and to secure it during moves.
- Get ramps/dollies: use a ramp to roll items into a trailer and a proper dolly to move them on the ground.
- Secure on trailer: fasten items down so they cannot shift while driving.
- Avoid twisting: keep your feet pointed where you want to go, lift with your legs, and pivot with your feet rather than twisting your torso.

Love,
Grandpa

Subject: Short submission — Miner’s cooking recipe booklet (c. 1942) with photo of page

Hello,

Please consider the following short submission for the community newspaper: a miner’s cooking recipe booklet dated c. 1942 was found tucked inside a coal camp trunk. The small hand‑stitched booklet contains simple, hearty recipes miners used to feed their families and crews during the war years. I am sending a photo of one booklet page with this submission.

Below is the recipe as printed in the booklet and attributed to miner William Daniels:

Coal Camp Stew — attributed to William Daniels
Ingredients:
- 2 lb meat (beef or salt pork recommended)
- 4–5 potatoes, peeled and quartered
- 2 carrots, sliced
- 1 onion, chopped
- 1 small cabbage, coarsely chopped
- 4 cups water or broth
- Salt and pepper to taste
- 1 bay leaf (optional)
- 1–2 tablespoons flour or biscuit crumbs to thicken (optional)

Method:
1. Cut meat into bite-sized pieces and brown if possible in a pot over medium heat.
2. Add onion and sauté briefly until softened.
3. Add potatoes, carrots, cabbage and water or broth to cover. Add bay leaf if using.
4. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer until vegetables and meat are tender, about 1–2 hours.
5. Season with salt and pepper. If a thicker stew is desired, stir in flour mixed with a little cold water or add biscuit crumbs and simmer a few minutes more.
6. Serve hot and share.

Attached: photo of the booklet page showing the recipe as printed.

Thank you for considering this piece for publication. Please let me know if you need a caption for the photo or any further details.

Best regards,
